newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lockheed to buy Russian rocket engines.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed to buy Russian rocket engines.

text.p: Lockheed Martin Corp. has ordered 101 rocket engines to be built in Russia for use on its new Atlas rocket, in a deal valued at more than $1.0 billion, the firm announced at the Paris airshow Tuesday.
The U.S. defence and aerospace group said it also hoped the engines would be selected for the U.S. government's expendable rocket programme.

Lockheed said a joint venture between Russia's NPO Energomash and U.S. engines maker Pratt & Whitney, part of United Technologies Corp., will co-produce the RD-180 engines under exclusive contract for Lockheed.
"We are committed to increased reliability, lower risk and lower cost on our new rocket series," said Mel Brashears, president of Lockheed's Space and Strategic Missiles division.
The engines will be built in Khimsky, Russia and be will be used on Lockheed's new Atlas IIAR rocket that is scheduled to be put into service late next year.
Atlas is launched by Lockeed's International Launch Services (ILS) division that also launches Russia's Proton rocket. ILS is a joint venture with Russian and Ukrainian companies.
ILS said it has 49 satellite launches on order, worth over $3 billion, and has now equalled the market share of its arch rival Europe's Arianespace that launches the Ariane rocket.
But Arianespace said its market share was bigger, contending that it would consider as options many of the contracts ILS claims as firm deals.

The new Atlas rocket is scheduled to take over four metric tons into geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) -- the orbit used on most large communications satellites. It will give Atlas the capacity to launch some of the heaviest commercial satellites now on the market.

The U.S. Air Force is developing the Evolved Expendable Launch Vehicle (EELV) series slated for its first launch in 2001. The rocket will be used for government and commercial payloads and is expected to eventually cut the cost of launching satellites by 80 percent.
The current price of launching satellites exceeds $25,000 per kilo and launch costs often exceed the cost of the satellite payloads.

Lockheed hopes the RD-180 engine will be selected for use on commercial missions using the EELV. "This all relates to commercial space," Brashears said. Legislation prohibits non-U.S. engines for use on government payloads. A supplier will be chosen in June 1998.

Industry sources were confident that demand for satellites and their launchers would remain strong -- particularly from booming Asia-Pacific rim countries, having seen actual launch rates increase by 75 percent from levels being predicted three years ago.
In addition to Atlas and Arianespace, both Boeing Co. and takeover target McDonnell Douglas plan to introduce more powerful rockets over the next 18 months.
